How did the harsh enforcement of vagrancy laws threaten to place African Americans into a new form of slavery?
1 Answer
Greg Brecht
, Writer, Floridian, Liberal,

It didn’t threaten to place African Americans into a new form of slavery. It did put them in new form of slavery.
The vagrancy laws were designed so that men could be picked up. They were then rented out, and the system has been called “convict leasing.” It provided a sizable part of local and state government revenue. A widely quoted figure is that in 1898, 73% of Alabama’s entire state revenue came from leasing convicts.
Convicts leased under this system worked on railroads, in factories and in mines. Convicts were treated poorly. The death rate was high. The system lasted until the 1920s, and was not finally abolished until 1941.
Nobody really paid any attention until a white boy from North Dakota got caught up in the system. He was whipped to death by a supervisor who had leased him.
The numbers were not huge, but in all the states combined over the years of the system, 100,000 victims is a reasonable guess, and 10,00 deaths also seems a reasonable guess.
It should be noted that such systems are not entirely dead. There are towns in Missouri and elsewhere that get 25% or more of their revenue from traffic tickets, with officers assigned quotas, and black drivers targeted. There is also a significant amount of prison labor in the US, supposedly volunteer, that ranges from no pay at all to a median of $3.45 a day. Prisons also tend to deduct certain kinds of expenses from the pay. In addition prisoners now in many places are being charged room and board.
The 13th Amendment does in fact allow involuntary servitude if it’s a punishment for a crime.

United States Vagrancy Laws
Risa L. Goluboff
and Adam Sorensen
https://doi.org/10.1093/acrefore/9780199329175.013.259
Published online: 20   December   2018
Summary
The crime of vagrancy has deep historical roots in American law and legal culture. Originating in 16th-century England, vagrancy laws came to the New World with the colonists and soon proliferated throughout the British colonies and, later, the United States. Vagrancy laws took myriad forms, generally making it a crime to be poor, idle, dissolute, immoral, drunk, lewd, or suspicious. Vagrancy laws often included prohibitions on loitering—wandering around without any apparent lawful purpose—though some jurisdictions criminalized loitering separately. Taken together, vaguely worded vagrancy, loitering, and suspicious persons laws targeted objectionable “out of place” people rather than any particular conduct. They served as a ubiquitous tool for maintaining hierarchy and order in American society. Their application changed alongside perceived threats to the social fabric, at different times and places targeting the unemployed, labor activists, radical orators, cultural and sexual nonconformists, racial and religious minorities, civil rights protesters, and the poor. By the mid-20th century, vagrancy laws served as the basis for hundreds of thousands of arrests every year. But over the course of just two decades, the crime of vagrancy, virtually unquestioned for four hundred years, unraveled. Profound social upheaval in the 1960s produced a concerted effort against the vagrancy regime, and in 1972, the US Supreme Court invalidated the laws. Local authorities have spent the years since looking for alternatives to the many functions vagrancy laws once served.
